question: A 74-year-old man with a history of encephalomyelitis, ataxia, and nystagmus a new diagnosis of small cell carcinoma of the lung (T2, N1, Mn/a) is admitted to the hospital due to painless loss of vision in his right eye. A full workup reveals optic neuritis and uveitis in the affected eye. Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be present in the serum of the patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Small cell carcinoma of the lung -> paraneoplastic syndrome -> autoimmune response -> production of specific antibodies -> Anti-Yo antibody -> 80% CHAIN: Encephalomyelitis, ataxia, and nystagmus -> paraneoplastic syndrome -> specific antibody production -> Anti-Yo antibody -> 75% CHAIN: Optic neuritis and uveitis -> autoimmune etiology -> specific antibody production -> Anti-Yo antibody -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely antibody to be present in the serum of the patient is Anti-Yo. The patient's history of encephalomyelitis, ataxia, nystagmus, optic neuritis, and uveitis all point towards an autoimmune etiology, potentially triggered by the small cell carcinoma of the lung. The presence of Anti-Yo antibodies is strongly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like the ones observed in this patient.
analysis: The patient's presentation of optic neuritis and uveitis in the setting of small cell carcinoma of the lung and a history of encephalomyelitis, ataxia, and nystagmus strongly suggests a paraneoplastic syndrome. Among the given options, Anti-Yo antibodies are most commonly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like the one observed in this patient. Anti-Yo antibodies are specifically linked to cerebellar degeneration, which aligns with the patient's symptoms.
